title: The Rhythm and the Silence: Vienna to Geneva by way of Hellerau
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Vienna and the Return to Geneva

stops.name: Vienna, birth in the clockmaker's household
stops.campa: Émile Henri Jaques is born in Vienna to a Swiss couple from Sainte-Croix, three generations of Vaudois pastors behind them: his father Jules represents the watchmakers of the Jura in the Austrian capital; his mother Julie Jaunin, trained in a Pestalozzi school, is herself a fine musician and teacher. From her he takes his first piano lessons at six, and with them the Pestalozzian conviction, planted before he can name it, that a child learns truly only through the body and the senses, never through the page alone.
suggested_refs: Portrait photograph of the infant Émile Jaques, Vienna, 1865-66

stops.name: Geneva, the Conservatoire de Musique
stops.campa: In 1875 the family leaves Vienna and settles in Geneva, the true country of the boy's blood. At twelve he enters the Conservatoire de Musique, where the ordinary curriculum of solfège and harmony sits on him like a coat cut for someone else: dutiful, correct, and strangely mute. He excels without being moved. Decades later he will say that these very years, in which technically able students could not feel what they played, planted the first suspicion that something essential to music was being taught to the ear and withheld from the whole body.
suggested_refs: The historic Conservatoire de Musique de Genève building, Place Neuve

stops.name: Geneva, the Belles-Lettres and La Soubrette
stops.campa: At sixteen, while still at university, he joins the Belles-Lettres literary society, Geneva's forge of young writers and performers, acting and composing among students who will remain his circle for life. That year he writes and stages his first operetta, La Soubrette, and founds a student orchestra he names Musigena. Music, theatre and comic invention are already inseparable in him: the same fusion that will, thirty years hence, be renamed eurhythmics and installed as a discipline in its own right.
suggested_refs: Belles-Lettres society records, University of Geneva archives

segments.name: Paris, Algiers, Vienna: the Making of a Musician

stops.name: Paris: the Comédie-Française, Delibes, Fauré
stops.campa: At nineteen he goes to Paris to complete his training on two fronts at once, as if music alone could not hold him: acting under the great players of the Comédie-Française, Talbot chief among them, and composition under Léo Delibes and the young Gabriel Fauré, with Marmontel at the piano. He writes a comic opera, Riquet à la Houppe, and lives the double life of actor and composer that will mark every later stage-work: the pageants, the operas, the civic Festspiele, where music, movement and speech are never quite separated.
suggested_refs: The Salle Richelieu of the Comédie-Française, where Talbot taught

stops.name: Algiers, assistant conductor at the Théâtre des Nouveautés
stops.campa: A post as second conductor under the composer Adler brings him to Algiers, and the colonial theatre's routine repertoire is not what he remembers of these months. Beyond the pit, in the streets and cafés of the city, he hears for the first time drumming and dance whose rhythmic patterns answer to no bar-line he has been taught: quintuple and septuple measures, phrases that breathe against the beat rather than inside it, the human body itself keeping a time no European stave can fix. He begins, unofficially, to notate what he hears.
suggested_refs: Musical transcriptions of Algerian rhythms attributed to Jaques-Dalcroze's Algiers notebooks

stops.name: Algiers, the theatre fails; a new name is taken
stops.campa: The Théâtre des Nouveautés goes bankrupt and the young conductor tours for a season with the scattering company rather than return at once to Europe, unwilling yet to let go of the rhythms that have unsettled him. It is in these Algiers years, chroniclers agree, that he adds Dalcroze to his birth name of Jaques: to be told apart from another composer of the same surname, but also, the canon likes to read, to mark the man who came home changed by a drum he cannot yet notate in any Conservatoire's terms.
suggested_refs: Théâtre des Nouveautés d'Alger, contemporary lithograph

stops.name: Vienna: Bruckner, Fuchs, Graedener
stops.campa: From the Algerian drum he returns, by way of Paris, to the city of his birth, and studies organ, piano and composition with Anton Bruckner, Robert Fuchs and Karl Graedener. Vienna gives him counterpoint and orchestration at the highest German bench; it does not touch what Algiers opened. He carries the two educations side by side, unreconciled, for the next five years: the strict harmonic science of the Conservatory and the wordless certainty that the body itself is a rhythmic instrument no harmony treatise addresses.
suggested_refs: The Vienna Conservatory (now the Universität für Musik) where Bruckner taught

stops.name: Paris, Mathis Lussy and the science of musical rhythm
stops.campa: Back in Paris he meets Mathis Lussy, the Swiss theorist who has spent a life writing on the mechanics of musical rhythm, accent and nuance. The encounter is decisive: Lussy gives him a vocabulary and a rigor for the intuition Algiers first planted, the sense that rhythm is a bodily and physiological fact before it is a notated one. Within three years, appointed to teach in Geneva, he will begin turning Lussy's analysis and his own Algerian memory into a classroom method no Conservatoire has yet imagined.
suggested_refs: Mathis Lussy, Traité de l'expression musicale (1874)

stops.name: Geneva, appointed Professor of Harmony
stops.campa: At twenty-seven he is named Professor of Harmony and solfège at the Conservatoire de Musique de Genève, the institution that once taught him so correctly and so incompletely. From the first term he watches his own old affliction repeat itself in his pupils: fingers fluent on the keyboard, ears trained to name every interval, and bodies that cannot walk a bar of triple time without stumbling. He begins, quietly, to experiment: testing exercises whose subject is not the ear alone but the whole standing, breathing, weight-bearing person.
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire de Musique de Genève faculty roll, 1892

stops.name: Geneva: the desks removed, the jersey and bare feet
stops.campa: The experiments harden into a doctrine. He clears the desks from his classroom and makes the students stand and step the beat while they sing; he asks for loose jersey and bare feet in place of corset and heeled shoe, arguing that the body cannot answer music truthfully in clothes built to restrain it. Method piled on method, tested and discarded and tested again: he will say of these Geneva years only that he built the whole edifice by trying, over and over, to find the particular cause of each pupil's particular deafness of limb.
stops.quote: It is by trying to discover the individual cause of each musical defect, and to find a means of correcting it, that I have gradually built up my method of eurhythmics. This method is entirely based upon experiments many times repeated.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, 'Rhythm as a Factor in Education', in Rhythm, Music and Education (trans. Ingham, 1921)
suggested_refs: Early photographs of barefoot rhythmic gymnastics classes, Geneva Conservatoire, c. 1900
sources: Gutenberg eBook 21653, The Eurhythmics of Jaques-Dalcroze

stops.name: Geneva, Poème alpestre at the National Exhibition
stops.campa: The Swiss National Exhibition opens on the Plaine de Plainpalais, and Jaques-Dalcroze is entrusted with the Poème alpestre, the official Festspiel of the fair: massed choirs, an orchestra, and a libretto of mountains and cowherds staged before thousands. It is his first great civic pageant, the form he will return to at every turning of his life, and already it fuses what the Conservatoire keeps separate: music, poetry, and the moving crowd as a single instrument of national feeling, rehearsed like a rhythmic-gymnastics class scaled to a whole canton.
suggested_refs: Poster of the Exposition nationale suisse, Geneva, 1896

stops.name: Geneva, marriage to Nina Faliero
stops.campa: On the day after Christmas he marries the Italian soprano Maria-Anna Starace, who sings under the stage name Nina Faliero and who will take leading roles in several of his own operas in the years ahead. The household she keeps becomes the quiet counterweight to the classroom battles at the Conservatoire: a working artist's marriage, music at both ends of the table, in the city that will, through every later upheaval, remain the fixed point he returns to.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Nina Faliero-Dalcroze in operatic costume, c. 1900

stops.name: Lausanne: the Festival Vaudois, canton's centenary
stops.campa: For the hundredth anniversary of the canton of Vaud's entry into the Confederation, Jaques-Dalcroze composes the Festival vaudois, a Festspiel to match the Poème alpestre in scale: the second of the great civic pageants that will punctuate his career, always at the hinge of a Swiss canton's or city's memory of itself. Choruses drawn from villages across the canton rehearse for months; the composer conducts the mass of amateur voices as he once tried to conduct fingers that could not keep time, and finds, in the crowd instead of the classroom, the same rhythmic problem at civic scale.
suggested_refs: Programme of the Festival vaudois, Lausanne, 1903

stops.name: Paris, Le Bonhomme Jadis and the letter from Appia
stops.campa: His opera Le Bonhomme Jadis is staged at the Paris Opéra-Comique the same year that the Genevan scenographer Adolphe Appia, who witnessed a rhythmic-gymnastics demonstration and could not shake it from his mind, writes to him unbidden. The two Swiss reformers, one remaking the stage's light and space, the other remaking the body that moves through it, begin a correspondence that will, within four years, build a theatre together at Hellerau. Each recognizes in the other's art the missing half of his own.
stops.quote: To restore rhythm to the body, to make music vibrate within it, as to make music an integral part of one's organism, to play with this marvellous keyboard which is the muscular and nervous system, to render plastically a thought measured in space as in time, that is what I seek.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, letter to Adolphe Appia, 1906 (trans. from the French; 'Rendre au corps son eurythmie...')
suggested_refs: Adolphe Appia's early stage-space sketches, 1906-1909
sources: opera-comique.com, 'La rythmique de Jaques-Dalcroze, entre pratique et utopie' (the 1906 letter to Appia, French text)

stops.name: Brussels, Les Jumeaux de Bergame at the Monnaie
stops.campa: The pantomime-ballet Les Jumeaux de Bergame is given at the Théâtre de la Monnaie, with Nina Faliero-Dalcroze among the singers: the composer's stage works now travelling beyond Switzerland and France into Belgium's first opera house. The reputation that carries him abroad is still, for the wider public, a composer's reputation; the rhythmic-gymnastics classroom in Geneva remains, to outsiders, a curious pedagogical sideline. Within two years the sideline will eclipse the composer, and a German garden-city will build him a theatre of his own.
suggested_refs: Théâtre Royal de la Monnaie, Brussels, programme 1908

stops.name: Geneva: a son, Gabriel, is born
stops.campa: A son, Gabriel, is born to Émile and Nina in Geneva: the household's own small rhythm added to the larger one the father is still building in classrooms and concert halls. Within a year the family's life will be pulled toward Saxony, as an invitation arrives from two German brothers, Wolf and Harald Dohrn, offering to build for the Geneva schoolmaster and his unruly pedagogy a garden-city temple of its own, with an unheard-of theatre attached, in a settlement called Hellerau.
suggested_refs: Gabriel Jaques-Dalcroze, family photograph, Geneva c. 1910

stops.name: Geneva, the Conservatoire calls it 'monkeyshines'
stops.campa: The Conservatoire's administrators, scandalized by bare feet and jersey tunics in a hall meant for scales and sonatas, condemn the rhythmic-gymnastics classes as undignified monkeyshines and press for their curtailment. At the very moment the door in Geneva narrows, the letter from Wolf Dohrn arrives from the new garden-city of Hellerau outside Dresden, proposing a Bildungsanstalt built to his exact specification: studios, gardens, no administrators to scandalize. He accepts. The method that Geneva tolerated as a sideline is about to be given its own state.
suggested_refs: Correspondence between Wolf Dohrn and Jaques-Dalcroze, 1909-10

stops.name: Hellerau, the Bildungsanstalt opens its doors
stops.campa: In the model garden-city of Hellerau above Dresden, reformed furniture, reformed dress, reformed bodies all manufactured on the same model estate, the Bildungsanstalt für rhythmische Gymnastik opens with 115 students crowded into still-unfinished rooms. Jaques-Dalcroze directs the whole curriculum himself: three fifty-minute morning classes in rhythmic movement, solfège and improvisation, afternoons of individual instruction and ensemble rehearsal, evenings of shared cultural life. The Conservatoire's sideline has become, almost overnight, the best-equipped school of its kind in Europe, and its founder its uncontested master.
stops.quote: The body can become a marvellous instrument of beauty and harmony when it vibrates in tune with artistic imagination and collaborates with creative thought.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, 'Rhythm as a Factor in Education', in Rhythm, Music and Education (trans. Ingham, 1921)
suggested_refs: The Bildungsanstalt Jaques-Dalcroze building, Hellerau, 1911

stops.name: Hellerau: Suzanne Perrottet, the Geneva assistant
stops.campa: Among his closest collaborators at the Bildungsanstalt is Suzanne Perrottet, the young Genevan violinist who trained under him at the Conservatoire and followed him to Saxony to teach his method to Hellerau's newest pupils, Mary Wigman among them. She is exact, gifted, and, though he does not yet see it, already restless inside the very discipline she teaches so well: movement always in service of a score, never sovereign over it. Within months she will be gone, drawn up the mountain above Ascona to a Hungarian who lets his dancers move in silence.
suggested_refs: Suzanne Perrottet teaching a Hellerau rhythmics class, 1911-12

stops.name: Hellerau: the Festspielhaus, dance as the handmaid of music
stops.campa: Under Adolphe Appia's white terraces and Alexander von Salzmann's walls of woven light, the new Festspielhaus opens its first Festspiele: two weeks of class demonstrations, the pantomime Echo et Narcisse, and, as its climax, the Descent into the Underworld from Gluck's Orphée, danced by Dalcroze's own students before some four thousand spectators and five hundred journalists drawn from every capital of Europe. Among the pupils absorbing the discipline of bar and phrase is a fierce, unfinished young woman named Marie Wiegmann, who will one day break the very obedience this stage teaches her.
stops.quote: I expect much from education in rhythm in elementary schools, provided it be given regularly, completely and sufficiently.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, Dresden lecture of 1912, in Rhythm, Music and Education (trans. Ingham, 1921)
suggested_refs: Appia's light-stage of the Festspielhaus Hellerau, Orpheus rehearsal photographs (1912-13)

stops.name: Hellerau, the pupil who wants the body itself to be the music
stops.campa: He does not fail to notice Marie Wiegmann's discontent. She is diligent, gifted, and increasingly mutinous, drilling rhythm into her spine as required while something unnamed in her strains against the method's first article of faith: that movement exists to serve the score. The painter Emil Nolde, watching her in class, tells her plainly to go to Rudolf von Laban, who teaches without music at all. Dalcroze loses her as he lost Perrottet, to the same mountain above Ascona; he will say only, of the pupils who leave this way, that the school could teach the discipline but not always contain what it woke.
suggested_refs: Emil Nolde, Kerzentänzerinnen (Candle Dancers, 1912)
mary_wigman.journey.json (shared pin, 'Nolde speaks the word Laban')

stops.name: Hellerau: the full Orfeo, and Jeanne Allemand takes her diploma
stops.campa: The second festival gives Gluck's Orfeo ed Euridice complete, Appia's terraces now fully realized in light and shadow; Prince Sergei Wolkonsky comes from the Imperial theatres, and the American teacher Susan Canfield among a wave of foreign visitors carries the method home across an ocean. Quietly, among the diploma students that same season, a young Genevan-trained pupil named Jeanne Allemand completes her rhythmics certificate and stays on to teach: the same Jeanne who will marry the painter Alexandre de Salzmann here and, within six years, carry a version of rhythmic discipline into a stranger school in Tiflis.
suggested_refs: Wolkonsky's account of the 1913 Hellerau festival

stops.name: Chamonix / Hellerau, the death of Wolf Dohrn
stops.campa: Wolf Dohrn, the visionary who built Hellerau for him and financed every year of it, dies in a skiing accident in the Chamonix Alps on 4 February 1914, descending from the Col de Balme in darkness, not yet thirty-six. Jaques-Dalcroze speaks the tribute at the funeral, gathered with the whole community of the garden-city he did not expect to bury its founder before its work was proven. Hellerau loses in an afternoon its driving force and its purse; the school Dohrn built will outlive him by a matter of months, not years.
suggested_refs: In Memoriam Hellerau (ed. Feudel, 1960), Dalcroze's funeral tribute to Dohrn
sources: researchgate.net, 'Appia, Jaques-Dalcroze, and Hellerau, Part Two'

segments.name: The Break: Reims and the Silence of Hellerau

stops.name: Geneva, a pageant for the Confederation's centenary
stops.campa: Commissioned three years earlier to mark the centenary of Geneva's entry into the Swiss Confederation, Jaques-Dalcroze returns from Hellerau in the spring of 1914 with his assistant Annie Beck and a cadre of senior students to rehearse La Fête de Juin: a Festspiel in five acts, libretto by Daniel Baud-Bovy and Albert Malche, built for a temporary theatre of 5,700 seats rising at the edge of the Perle du Lac park. He does not yet know he is leaving Hellerau for good; he believes, like everyone that spring, that he will simply go back after the summer.
suggested_refs: Plans of the temporary Théâtre du Centenaire, Mon-Repos, Geneva, 1914
sources: lapartoche.blogspot.com, 'La Fête de juin, un spectacle patriotique genevois en 1914'

stops.name: Geneva: La Fête de Juin, a city becomes a chorus
stops.campa: Over eight performances at the Théâtre du Centenaire, more than a thousand performers and a full symphony orchestra enact the four centuries of Geneva's road into the Swiss Confederation before packed grandstands on the shore of the lake. It is the summit of his civic-pageant art, larger than the Poème alpestre and the Festival vaudois combined, and it is an immense and undisputed triumph: the last entirely happy season, the canon will note, before Europe's own rhythm breaks beyond anyone's power to compose it.
suggested_refs: Vintage poster, 'La Fête de Juin, Centenaire de l'entrée de Genève dans la Confédération Suisse', 1914
sources: galerie123.com, poster archive, 'La Fête de Juin' 1914
lapartoche.blogspot.com, 'La Fête de juin, un spectacle patriotique genevois en 1914'

stops.name: Geneva, the war breaks over the summer's triumph
stops.campa: Within weeks of the Fête de Juin's last curtain, the Archduke's assassination at Sarajevo detonates the general war, and Germany's armies cross into Belgium and France. Jaques-Dalcroze and Harald Dohrn, Wolf's brother, try for a time by letter to imagine how the Hellerau school might be restored once the fighting stops; neither man yet grasps that it will not stop for four years, and that the man who built the theatre for him is barely six months in his grave. Geneva, neutral and watching, becomes for the second time in a year his only fixed ground.
suggested_refs: Swiss mobilization notices, Geneva, August 1914

stops.name: Geneva, news of the burning of Reims
stops.campa: On 19 September German shells set the roof of Reims Cathedral alight: the coronation church of Clovis and of Charles VII, the stone the whole French-speaking world reads as the nation's own crown. Geneva's papers carry the news within days, and French-speaking Switzerland's writers and artists move to protest: Jaques-Dalcroze, who has built his life's second half on German soil and among German patrons, adds his signature to the lists the Tribune de Genève will publish through the autumn, alongside the painter Ferdinand Hodler and dozens of others who had, until this month, called Germany a second home.
suggested_refs: Bibliothèque de Genève, 'Protestation des écrivains, artistes et savants suisses contre le bombardement de la cathédrale de Reims'
joan_of_arc.journey.json (Reims Cathedral, shared coordinates)
sources: bge-geneve.ch, iconographie, 'Protestation... contre le bombardement de la cathédrale de Reims'
mahmah.ch, 'Hodler et Dalcroze: une histoire d'harmonie'

stops.name: Geneva: barred from Germany, Hellerau falls silent
stops.campa: The signature on the Reims protest is remembered in Germany, and the man who ran Hellerau's school for four years is quietly barred from re-entering the country that built it for him. The Bildungsanstalt, already bereft of Dohrn's money and now of its own director, cannot survive the war and folds within the year. Jaques-Dalcroze will never set foot in Hellerau again. What Reims cost the stone of a cathedral, it costs him a garden-city and a theatre; he does not recant the signature, and Geneva, once more, absorbs what Germany has let fall.
suggested_refs: Closure records of the Bildungsanstalt Jaques-Dalcroze, Hellerau, 1914-15
sources: mahmah.ch, 'Hodler et Dalcroze: une histoire d'harmonie'

stops.name: Geneva, the Institut opens at the Terrassière
stops.campa: A subscription committee of Geneva citizens, determined not to lose the creator of rhythmics a second time, raises the funds for a new Institut Jaques-Dalcroze, which opens its doors in the former Salle de la Source on the Rue de la Terrassière. What Hellerau built in brick and light-stage, Geneva rebuilds in rented rooms and civic will; the method that a German garden-city once housed so lavishly returns, chastened by the war but intact, to the city of his marriage, his son, and his first Conservatoire post.
suggested_refs: Institut Jaques-Dalcroze, Rue de la Terrassière 44, Geneva, the school-house since 1915

stops.name: Geneva: Les Premiers Souvenirs, the Institut's own pageant
stops.campa: With the war still grinding on beyond the neutral border, the young Institut mounts its own inaugural spectacle, Les premiers souvenirs, text by Jacques Chenevière set to Jaques-Dalcroze's music: a modest civic pageant beside the Fête de Juin's thousand performers, but proof that the Terrassière school is no mere refugee camp for a broken German enterprise. It has its own stage, its own rites, its own graduating dancers. The method has found, at last, a home that cannot be closed by a foreign war office.
suggested_refs: Programme of Les premiers souvenirs, Institut Jaques-Dalcroze, Geneva 1918

stops.name: Geneva, La Fête de la Jeunesse et de la Joie
stops.campa: Nine years after the Fête de Juin, he composes a new civic pageant, La Fête de la Jeunesse et de la Joie, the festival of youth and joy, with Nina Faliero-Dalcroze again among the principal performers. Where the 1914 pageant carried the freight of a nation's history, this one is offered as a plain gift to a Europe still nursing its wounds: youth and gladness staged as antidotes, deliberately, to the four years just past. The pattern of his life is now fixed: Geneva calls him for its great civic occasions as automatically as it once doubted his bare-footed classroom.
suggested_refs: Programme of La Fête de la Jeunesse et de la Joie, Geneva 1923

stops.name: Geneva and Paris: honorary citizen, a Paris branch
stops.campa: On 21 November 1925 the Republic and Canton of Geneva names him an honorary citizen: the sixty-year-old Vienna-born son of a clock-salesman formally adopted, in full civic ceremony, by the city that took his family in fifty years before. The same year sees a Paris branch of the Institut established, carrying the Terrassière's teaching into France proper; rhythmics, once a scandal to one Conservatoire, is now exported by two nations at once, taught by disciples who scatter from Geneva to London, Stockholm, Chicago, wherever a school will have them.
suggested_refs: Certificate of honorary citizenship (bourgeois d'honneur), Geneva, 1925

stops.name: Geneva, the First International Congress on Rhythm
stops.campa: The Institut convenes the first International Congress on Rhythm, drawing teachers, physicians and educators from across Europe to debate a discipline that, fourteen years after Hellerau, has outgrown any single school's authority over it. He presides as an elder statesman of a movement he began virtually alone in a Geneva harmony class, watching younger disciples, some trained under his own hand, some at one remove through Laban's and Wigman's rival schools of Ausdruckstanz, argue over a doctrine of the body that has by now split into several irreconcilable churches.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the First International Congress on Rhythm, Geneva, 1926

stops.name: Geneva, Officer of the Légion d'honneur
stops.campa: France, whose Opéra-Comique staged his youthful operas and whose Reims cathedral he protested for, names him Officer of the Légion d'honneur, adding a French decoration to the Swiss honorary citizenship of four years before. The double honor closes, formally, the wound the Reims protest opened with Germany: the republic he defended in September 1914 now decorates the man who signed against its enemy's guns. He is sixty-four, and the Institut he founded amid the ashes of Hellerau has by now trained a generation that will carry rhythmics through a second war he cannot yet foresee.
suggested_refs: Légion d'honneur citation for Jaques-Dalcroze, 1929

segments.name: The Last Years and the Silence

stops.name: Geneva: a second war, a neutral shore
stops.campa: France falls and the Institut's Paris branch is cut off; Geneva, neutral again as it was in 1914, becomes once more his only unbroken ground. At seventy-five he no longer teaches daily, but the Terrassière school he built from a war's wreckage keeps its doors open through blackout and ration, training children and refugees alike in a discipline that asks nothing more of a body than that it learn to feel its own time. He publishes his memoir, Souvenirs, notes et critiques, that same wartime season, setting down at last, from Vienna to Algiers to Hellerau, the whole rhythm of a life spent teaching rhythm.
suggested_refs: Jaques-Dalcroze, Souvenirs, notes et critiques (Attinger, Neuchâtel, 1942)

stops.name: Geneva, the laurels of old age
stops.campa: In the years after the second war's end the honors come one after another, as if the world wished to settle its account before it was too late: an honorary doctorate from the University of Lausanne in 1945, another from Clermont-Ferrand in 1948, and from his own city of Geneva that same year, the University conferring on its eighty-three-year-old citizen the degree it never thought to offer the young harmony teacher whose bare-footed classes it once found scandalous. He accepts each with the same plain courtesy he has shown every pupil since 1892.
suggested_refs: Honorary doctorate diplomas, Lausanne 1945 and Geneva 1948

stops.name: Geneva: death, and burial at the Cimetière des Rois
stops.campa: He dies in Geneva on 1 July 1950, five days short of his eighty-fifth birthday, and is buried in the Cimetière des Rois, the city's resting place for its most honored dead. The Institut on the Terrassière continues without him, as Hellerau once tried and failed to continue; the method he built from a mother's Pestalozzian conviction, an Algiers drum, and a Conservatoire's stumbling fingers has by now crossed every ocean his pupils were willing to cross. Geneva, which took in the Vienna-born family of a clock-salesman in 1875, keeps him in its ground for good.
suggested_refs: Grave of Émile Jaques-Dalcroze, Cimetière des Rois, Geneva
